In this lesson You will learn What are rates and unit rates? How do we use unit rates in daily life? How do we use unit rates in math? How to calculate averages? Applying basic Statistics

Words to know

Average — number that is typical of a group of numbers

Mean — sum of all the numbers in a set divided by the total number of numbers in that set

Median — number in the center of a set of numbers when they are arranged from smallest to largest

Mode — most common number in a set of numbers

Range — spread of difference between the lowest and highest numbers in a set

Rate — amount of something measured in two different units, such as when you say soup costs $5 for 6 cans

Round — make a number simpler but keep it close to its original number

Speed — measure of how fast or slow something is moving

Unit Rate — comparison of two measures when one of the measures is set at one unit, such as when you say you walk at 3 miles per hour

What are Rates? Rates compare two related amounts. The two amounts are measured in different units.

For example, imagine you are in a store where a half–gallon container of milk costs $3.06. The rate is $3.06 for a half gallon. You can say “$3.06 per half gallon.”

Per means for each .

Unit Rates Rates are easier to compare if one of the amounts is a single unit. A unit rate is a rate where one of the quantities is equal to one. Instead of giving just the price for a half–gallon, the store could tell you the price for one whole gallon or even for just one fluid ounce.

Price per fluid ounce and per gallon are unit rates. When the rate is per fluid ounce or per gallon, it’s much easier to compare and understand prices. The store sign would tell you the milk costs 4¢ per fluid ounce, or $5.12 a gallon. In math, we can show this as 4¢/fl oz or $5.12/gal. Then you could go to another shop where the milk was 3¢/fl oz. You would know the milk costs less, whatever size the container was.

When the second number is one, you do not have to write the number one. For example, “Miles per hour” means “miles per one hour”, and “Cookies per student” means “cookies per one student.”

Unit rates are a crucial concept in math, particularly for GED students, as they help simplify comparisons and problem-solving. Here are some basic examples of unit rates:

Example 1: Speed

Problem: A car travels 150 miles in 3 hours. What is the unit rate in miles per hour? Solution: {$ \text{Unit Rate} = \frac{150 \text{ miles}}{3 \text{ hours}} = 50 \text{ miles per hour} $}

Example 2: Price per Item

Problem: A pack of 8 batteries costs $12. What is the unit price per battery? Solution: {$ \text{Unit Rate} = \frac{12 \text{ dollars}}{8 \text{ batteries}} = 1.5 \text{ dollars per battery} $}

Example 3: Cost per Weight

Problem: A 5-pound bag of apples costs $10. What is the cost per pound? Solution: {$ \text{Unit Rate} = \frac{10 \text{ dollars}}{5 \text{ pounds}} = 2 \text{ dollars per pound} $}

Example 4: Fuel Efficiency

Problem: A car uses 15 gallons of gasoline to travel 300 miles. What is the fuel efficiency in miles per gallon? Solution: {$ \text{Unit Rate} = \frac{300 \text{ miles}}{15 \text{ gallons}} = 20 \text{ miles per gallon} $}

Example 5: Earnings per Hour

Problem: A person earns $120 for 8 hours of work. What is the hourly wage? Solution: {$ \text{Unit Rate} = \frac{120 \text{ dollars}}{8 \text{ hours}} = 15 \text{ dollars per hour} $}

Example 6: Heart Rate

Problem: A heart beats 150 times in 2 minutes. What is the heart rate in beats per minute? Solution: {$ \text{Unit Rate} = \frac{150 \text{ beats}}{2 \text{ minutes}} = 75 \text{ beats per minute}$}

Video: Using Unit Rates VIDEO TRANSCRIPT + Using unit rates in your math test Unit rates will come up in your math test. The questions that use unit rates are mostly word problems. Not all rates will be given as unit rates. You may need to change the rate to a unit rate to solve a problem. Let's try this question: ■ Check for understanding Klaus rode his bike 6 kilometers to work. The ride took him 20 minutes. Eugenia rode her bike 4 kilometers to work in 15 minutes. Who was riding faster? Work : These two numbers are hard to compare without changing into a unit rate. So let’s convert the rates to unit rates. First, calculate how far Klaus rode per minute. When you see the word per , it is a useful signal that you may need to divide. You can write Klaus’s speed as 6 km/20 minutes, or 6/20. The first step is to divide 6 by 20 = 0.3. Klaus was traveling 0.3 kilometers per minute. Now calculate Eugenia’s speed. Divide 4 by 15 = 0.27 Eugenia was traveling 0.27 kilometers per minute. The calculator shows “.26667.” We round the answer up to 0.27 so that it is easier to write and calculate. Eugenia’s speed is approximately 0.27 kilometers per minute. Answer : Klaus was faster. He traveled 0.3 km/min and Eugenia traveled only 0.27 km/min. Applying basics Statistics One skill you will need for your test is being able to calculate an average . An average is a number that represents a bigger group of numbers. It can be the middle number (called the median ), the most popular number (called the mode ), or the one that gives you the best idea of the group (the mean ). In your test, you will probably have to calculate the mean of a group of numbers. A group of numbers is called a set. One more term to know about: the range in averages means the spread, or difference between the lowest and highest numbers. In our example set (6, 8, 8, 8, 10, 11, 12) the range is the difference between 6 and 12. To calculate the range, subtract the lowest number from the highest number: 12 – 6 = 6. So how will these terms and calculations come up in your test? Finding the mean is the most likely to come up, but it’s good to remember how to find a mode and median, too. You may get a word problem, or you may get sets of numbers in a table, or you may get a question with a combination of both. Mean - Add up all the numbers in the set and divide by how many numbers you have Example : Find the mean of the 3 numbers 5, 6, and 10. First add them together (5 + 6 + 10 = 21). Then divide by the number of numbers in the set, which is 3: 21 /3 = 7. The mean is 7. Median - once the list of numbers are in order, from least to the greatest, the median is the middle number. If there's an even amount of numbers, then average the two middle numbers, to find the median Example : In a group of children, ages 6, 8, 8, 8, 10, 11, and 12, the median is 8. Half the numbers are one side of the median, and half the numbers are on the other side. If you have an even number of numbers, the median will be halfway between the two middle numbers. You will have to add the two middle numbers and divide by 2 to get the median. Mode - the number that repeats the most in a set. If there are not any repeated numbers in a set, then there is no mode. In this lesson You will learn What are ratios and how do we use them? What does proportion mean? What are equivalent fractions? How do we use fractions to calculate proportions? How are proportions used in real life? What are scale and scale factors?

Words to know Equivalent Fractions — fractions that have the same value and might be written with different denominators (example: ½ and 2/4 are equivalent fractions)

Legend — key or explanation on a map

Outcome — how something turns out, or the result

Probability — how likely something is to happen

Proportion — amount or share of something compared to a whole

Proportional — having a size, number, or amount that is directly related to or appropriate for something.

Scale — smaller (or larger) version of an object that is proportional to the original object

Scale Factor — ratio of a bigger object or quantity to a smaller object or quantity

What are Ratios A ratio describes a relationship between two amounts or things.

When you make bread, there is a specific ratio of one ingredient to another ingredient. For example, you may use 15 ounces of flour and 5 ounces of fat to make 20 tortillas. We say the ratio of flour to fat is 15 to 5.

Tortilla is a South American bread

The ratio of ingredients is the same whether you make 4 tortillas, 8 tortillas, or 100 tortillas. It stays the same while the amount changes. Ratios are like rates, which you learned about in the last lesson. A rate such as price per apple is the same for 3 apples or 6 apples. In the same way, the ratio in the tortilla recipe is the same for 3 tortillas or 6 tortillas.

(:)

In math symbols, the colon (:) is used instead of the word to . The ratio of flour to fat is 15:5. It can be reduced to 3:1 . You could use any amount of flour and fat and the ratio stays at 3:1.

Sometimes the word part is used in ratios because the units do not matter for a ratio (as long as they are the same as each other). For every one part of fat, you will need three parts (three times that amount) of flour. The recipe is in ounces, but the ratio will be the same even if we measure in grams. It will still be 3:1.

Proportions Proportions compare a quantity to a whole. When you reduce fractions, they still have the same proportion of the whole.

For example:

{$\frac{1}{2}$} is the same as {$\frac{2}{4}$} or {$\frac{3}{6}$} or {$\frac{50}{100}$}.

All have a value of 1/2, even though they are written with different numbers in the numerator and denominator. They are equivalent fractions because the proportions are the same. Equivalent means something of the same value, or equal.

A proportion can be written in several ways:

• Using fractions: {$(\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d})$}

• Using colons: (a:b = c:d)

• Using words: "a is to b as c is to d"

Example 1: Simple Proportion

Imagine you have a recipe that requires 2 cups of flour for every 3 cups of sugar. This can be written as the ratio 2:3.

Example 2: Proportions in Geometry

Proportions are also useful in geometry. Suppose two triangles are similar, and the sides of the first triangle are 3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm. The corresponding sides of the second triangle are 6 cm, 8 cm, and 10 cm. The proportions between corresponding sides of similar triangles are equal.

GED Exam Tip Exam tip The fun thing about proportions is that as long as you follow a pattern, you can not go wrong in setting up a proportion. There are many equivalent proportions that look different, but are solved using the same techniques, and give you the same answers. The following illustrations are just a few examples. {$\frac{20}{15}=\frac{b}{a}$} {$\frac{a}{b}=\frac{15}{20}$} {$\frac{20}{b}=\frac{15}{a}$} {$\frac{a}{15}=\frac{b}{20}$} 20a=15b

Using Proportions and Ratios Proportions and ratios are used in math problems. They are used to figure out something you don’t know from something you do know. You may have to apply a rate or ratio to find a missing proportion. So we’ll learn how to do that.

To solve a proportion, we apply the information we already know. Then we multiply or divide to find the missing proportion.

Let’s try with an example:

QUESTION : It costs $6.75 to buy three drinks at the mall. How much does 9 drinks cost?

We will solve this problem step by step:

Step 1: Set up the proportion. Write the rate that you know. It equals the rate that we want to find. Remember to write the numbers so the units match. The unit in the numerator should be the same unit on both sides of the equal sign.

{$\frac{$6.75}{3 drinks} = \frac{x dollas}{9 drinks}$}

Step 2: Compare the two equivalent fractions. How can you multiply or divide to find the second number from the first? You can cross multiply, as the video showed. Or you can just multiply the top by the same amount as the bottom. Either way, the proportions will be the same. In this case, the denominator on the left is multiplied by 3 in the denominator on the right.

Step 3 : Do the same operation to find the missing number. We multiplied the denominator by 3.

So, multiply the numerator by 3: 6.75 x 3 = 20.25. So x = $20.25

Answer: 9 drinks cost $20.25

Solving for a Ratio To solve a ratio the first thing to remember is that a ratio of “1 to 4” is composed of 5 parts. It is not the same as ¼ part of a whole.

It is important to keep track of the total and compare the number of parts.

Example: Find the ratio of yellow parts on the wheel.

2 yellow parts out of 6. 4 parts are not yellow. The ratio is 2:4 or 1 to 2 where yellow is ■ of the whole circle, which is not a ratio because it is not compared to the other parts.

Video: Proportions and Scales in Real Life Watch the video. Then answer the optional quiz next.

VIDEO TRANSCRIPT + Proportions and scale in real life Proportions are used in life for several different reasons. For example, we use proportions to make a small model of a building or ship, and we use proportions to draw a map. Just like ratios and unit rates, the proportions stay the same at different sizes. Scale models are small models of an original. Scale means a bigger or smaller version of the same thing. Proportional means having parts that are the correct or appropriate size in relation to each other. If you have ever used a map, then you already have experience with scale. Objects on a map are, of course, smaller than they are in real life. However, the sizes of roads and other objects on a map are proportional. We say the map is drawn to scale. This image shows a legend from a map. The legend explains the map’s symbols and shows the scale being used. The scale shows measurements for 32 miles and 32 kilometers. The map may use 1 inch to show 10 miles, for example. So the scale of the map would be one inch to 10 miles. Using

scale in word problems You may need to solve a word problem in your test to show you understand about scale. Here is an example: Juan is constructing a model of his favorite ship, the Cutty Sark. The Cutty Sark is 280 feet long and 35 feet wide. Juan only has enough wood to make his model 4 feet long. How wide will the model be? To answer, use proportions. Set up equivalent fractions. {$\color{Blue} \frac{length of model}{length of ship}=\frac{width of model}{width of ship}$} The numerators measure the model. The denominators measure the original ship. In this case you will need to divide to find w. To find w, divide the top by the same amount as the bottom. That way, the proportions will be the same. {$\color{Blue} \frac{4}{280}=\frac{w}{35}$} In this case, the denominator on the left is divided by 8 to get the denominator on the right. {$\frac{280}{35}=8$}. So you need to divide the top by 8 to keep the proportions the same: {$\frac{4}{8}=0.5$} The width of the model is 0.5 or ½ a foot, which is six inches. So w = 6 inches. Scale factor In the problem above, the scale is the length of the model divided by the length of the ship. The same scale applies to the width because the model is proportional to the real ship. You might get a question that asks you to calculate the scale factor. The scale factor is the ratio, or the relationship between the two sizes. After we answered the question, we had two equivalent fractions: {$\frac{4}{280}=\frac{0.5}{35}$}. They have the same scale. We could say the scale is 280 to 4, but we can simplify to understand the scale more clearly. {$\frac{4}{280}$} and {$\frac{0.5}{35}$}are the same as {$\frac{1}{70}$}. The model is 1/70th of the original. Now we can picture it better: the actual ship is 70 times bigger than Juan’s model! The scale is 70 to 1. You can show a scale factor like a ratio: 70:1.

Applications with Probability People often try to predict what is going to happen. But how can they know? What tools do they use? They may use their past experience or expert knowledge. But quite often they use math. Using math to predict an outcome is called calculating probability .

The outcome you are trying to find is called the favorable outcome. The formula for calculating probability is simple: You divide the number of favorable outcomes by the number of possible outcomes, so the formula looks like this:

{$\frac{\text{number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{number of possible outcomes}}$}

Imagine 5 pens of different colors, including green. You want the green pen, but you have to choose without looking.

What is the probability of choosing the one pen you want out of five?

The probability is 1 out of 5, or 1/5.

Practice Question Let’s try example with a question adapted from the GED practice test:

A house has a large window made of 15 equal–sized panes of glass. Three window panes have stars stuck on them.

If a ball thrown by mistake hits the window, what is the probability that the ball hits a window pane with a star on it?

Apply the formula:

{$\frac{\text{number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{number of possible outcomes}}$}

The number of favorable outcomes is 3 because there are 3 window panes with stars. The number of possible outcomes is 15 because there are a total of 15 window panes. That gives you a probability of 3/15, or 1/5.

If you are trying to get two favorable outcomes in just two tries, the probability is much smaller. What are chances of a ball hitting the same window pane twice by mistake? Without aiming the ball, the probability of hitting any window pane once 1/15. The probability of hitting it a second time without aiming is also 1/15. But the probability of doing it twice in a row without aiming is much smaller. That’s because there are many more possible outcomes for two events than for one. There is a formula for that too! It is:

{$\frac{\text{number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{number of possible outcomes}*{\text{number of possible outcomes}}}$}

If we apply the formula to our window pane problem, the chances of hitting the same windowpane twice in two throws is

{$\frac{1}{15*15}=\frac{1}{225}$}

So, the probability of the ball hitting a windowpane with a star on it is, 1 out of 225.

Vocabulary review Equivalent Fractions — fractions that have the same value and might be written with different denominators (example: ½ and 2/4 are equivalent fractions)

Legend — key or explanation on a map

Outcome — how something turns out, or the result

Probability — how likely something is to happen

Proportion — amount or share of something compared to a whole

Proportional — having a size, number, or amount that is directly related to or appropriate for something.

Scale — smaller (or larger) version of an object that is proportional to the original object

Scale Factor — ratio of a bigger object or quantity to a smaller object or quantity

Summary What we learned A ratio describes a relationship between two amounts or things. Proportions compare a quantity to a whole. If you apply the same ratio to two different quantities, they have the same proportions. Equivalent fractions are fractions with different numbers but the same proportions, such as 1/4 and 4/16. The units in proportions need to be the same in the numerator and the same in the denominator. You can use fractions to find proportions by applying the amounts you do know to find the ones you don't. Review Multi–step Word Problems and Inequalities About this lesson All the way through this math class, you’ve been solving equations and word problems while answering questions with several steps. In this lesson, we will review all those skills. You will also learn about a mathematical expression called an inequality. An inequality is similar to an equation, but it shows two sides where one side is greater or smaller than to the other side. You will also learn about the symbols used in inequality expressions. You may already know about these topics. If you do, just read quickly through the lesson. Then take the quiz to go to the next lesson.

Words to know Inequality — mathematical expression or sentence that is like an equation but shows you that one side is greater or smaller than the other

Word problem — a math question written as one sentence or more that requires learners to apply their math knowledge to a 'real-life' scenario

In this lesson You will learn How to solve inequalities? How to approach word problems? How to answer questions with several steps?

How Inequalities are Used An equal symbol (=) shows things are the same, or equal. You may have seen these symbols used instead of the equal sign: < > ≥ ≤. These symbols show inequalities. They tell you that values may not be equal on either side of the symbol. Inequalities are used for comparison as well as determining a range of value greater than or less than a known value.

Inequality Symbols Explained

• Equal to (=): This symbol indicates that the values on either side of the symbol are exactly the same. Example: 5=5, which reads "five is equal to five."

• Greater than (>): This symbol indicates that the value on the left is larger than the value on the right. Example: 5>3, which reads "five is greater than three."

• Less than (<): This symbol indicates that the value on the left is smaller than the value on the right. Example: 2<4, which reads "two is less than four."

• Greater than or equal to (≥): This symbol indicates that the value on the left is either greater than or exactly equal to the value on the right. Example: 7≥7, which reads "seven is greater than or equal to seven" and 8 ≥ 7, "eight is greater than or equal to seven."

• Less than or equal to (≤): This symbol indicates that the value on the left is either less than or exactly equal to the value on the right. Example: 6≤6 and 5≤6, which read "six is less than or equal to six" and "five is less than or equal to six. You can also find these, and more signs, at this link

Inequalities Using the Symbol Tool Before moving on, look over this GED Symbol Tool Resource . Let’s use the inequalities symbols to compare Whole Numbers.

• = ..is equal too 16 = 16 and –7 = –7

• < ..is less than 14 < 25 and -5<0

• ≤ ..is less than or equal to 38 ≤ 39

• > ..is greater than 17 > 14 and –5 > –9

• ≥ ..is greater than or equal to 26 ≥ 20

How to Approach Word Problems Your first and most important step is to understand the question. With a word problem, that means reading the words until you understand what math problem to do.

We’ll use a very simple question as an example.

Example:

Martina drinks 2 cups of tea each day, and she drinks twice as much water as tea. How much water does she drink in one week?

To find out how much water she drinks in one week:

• Tea per day : 2 cups

• Water per day : Since she drinks twice as much water, that's 2×2=4. So, she drinks 4 cups of water per day. Now, multiply the daily amount of water by the number of days in a week: 4 cups of water per day×7 days=28 cups of water per week. So, Martina drinks 28 cups of water in one week.

Tips to Solving Word Problems Here are some strategies you can use to solve a word problem.

1. Look at the Answer Choices First Before solving the problem, check the answer choices. This will give you clues about what’s expected:

• Do you need to find an exact number?

• Or are you just setting up the equation but not solving it?

You can often eliminate some choices right away if they don’t make sense. By reviewing the answer options, you can also figure out what steps might be needed—like working backward or recognizing that you need square units for an area.

2. Plan Your Steps Once you understand the question, think about what formulas or methods you need. You’ve likely practiced them in other lessons. Make sure you know how to access them during the test. It helps to plan your approach step by step before starting to solve.

3. Plug in What You Know Use the information given in the problem to fill in any blanks. You might need to follow a formula, or you may need to set up your own equation. It’s okay to write down notes or even draw pictures to help you visualize the problem. On the test, you’ll have a board to make notes and do calculations. Writing out your problem can help you clearly see what operation (addition, subtraction, etc.) is needed next.

Click here if you want to see an example of the above + Word Problem: Martina is organizing a party and needs to buy drinks. She plans to buy water and juice. For every 2 bottles of juice she buys, she wants to buy 3 bottles of water. Altogether, she wants to buy 20 bottles of drinks. Question: How many bottles of water does Martina need to buy? Answer Choices: A) 8 B) 10 C) 12 D) 15 Steps to Solve: 1. Look at the Answer Choices : The problem asks how many bottles of water Martina should buy. You know the total number of bottles (20) and the ratio between water and juice. Some answer choices can be eliminated if they don’t match that ratio. 2. Figure Out Your Steps : You can set up a ratio based on the information provided: For every 2 bottles of juice, there are 3 bottles of water. Preparing for your Math Test and Final Practice Quiz About this lesson You have learned many math skills in this class! This last lesson will prepare you to take your test. We’ll review what you need to know and give you some last tips. For example, you will review the skills of adding, multiplying, subtracting, and dividing. You will also review working with fractions, decimals, and exponents. In this lesson, you will also learn how to use strategies like back-solving, eliminating, and estimating to help you choose the correct answers in the GED Math Exam. And you will practice these skills by taking a short quiz.

Words to know Back–solve — plug an answer into a question to see if it is the correct one

Eliminate — get rid of the choices that are obviously incorrect

Estimate — make a quick calculation to get an approximate value or answer

Guess — give an answer without knowing for sure it is correct

Math Topics to Know You will want to make sure you understand the math topics in the list below. These are topics we have covered either in the lessons or in test tips. If there is something on this list you do not remember, go back and find the lesson on that topic:

Basic Arithmetic Operations

• Adding, multiplying, subtracting, and dividing whole numbers

• Adding, multiplying, subtracting, and dividing decimals

• Adding, multiplying, subtracting, and dividing fractions Number Theory and Properties

• Multiples, factors, and common factors

• Absolute value

• Distributive property

• Equivalent expressions

• Exponent rules

• Squares, cubes, and roots

• Undefined expressions Ratios, Proportions, and Percents

• Unit rates and converting units of measure

• Scale factors, ratios, and proportions

• Percentages Geometry

• Number lines

• Area and perimeter of shapes

• Pythagorean Theorem

• Volume and surface area of shapes Data and Statistics

• Data shown on graphs and tables

• Ordered pairs

• Averages (mean, median, mode, and range)

• Probability of simple and compound events

• Algebra

• Inputs, outputs, and functions

• Polynomials

• Equations and inequalities

With these math skills, you will be prepared for the questions on your math test.

Taking Your Math Test Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

VIDEO TRANSCRIPT + All along, you have been practicing for your test. You have answered questions at the end of each lesson. There will be questions like these on your test. The GED® math test is 115 minutes long and has two parts: Part 1 – (first 5 test questions) calculator not allowed Part 2 – (remaining 41 test questions) calculator allowed Students must submit their answers to the first 5 questions before moving on to the rest of the test. For part 2, you can bring a TI-30XS Multiview Scientific calculator or use the calculator on your computer screen (also known as the on-screen calculator). You can also use a formula sheet during the test. These parts are not timed separately. Here are some tips to keep in mind for the day of the exam Use shortcuts, calculators when allowed, and the formula sheets. Eliminating means getting rid of something. Eliminating answers in your test means to first cross off the answers that are obviously wrong. Estimating is a kind of guessing, but you are also using your math skills. Here is an example, you have a question for which you think the answer is between 20 and 25. That is your estimate. The answer choices are 0.2, 23, –23, and 735. Only one of the choices is between 20 and 25, so you can choose that one. If you are sure that your estimation is correct, you can move on to the next question. If you are not quite sure, don’t forget about back–solving, which we covered earlier in a test tip. You can use back–solving with most multiple–choice questions to test your choice. Back–solving is good for equations because sometimes it’s quicker to plug in a few answers and test them than to solve a problem from the beginning. If you already rejected some answers because of eliminating or estimating, you may only need to test one or two answers anyway. Guessing is

what you may have to do when you are running out of time and there are a few questions unanswered. If you don’t know how to answer the question, take a guess! Wrong answers do not count against you and your guess might be right! However, save your guessing until the end. Pay attention to the time The strategy of solving the easy problems first and then returning to the hard problems will help you use your testing time well. First answer the questions that seem easy to you. That way, you will be able to answer a higher number of questions than if you spent a lot of time on the harder questions. Then return to answer the harder questions and pay attention to the amount of time you have left. Do not spend all your time on the first couple of questions. You will feel rushed at the end if you have a lot of questions to answer. Watch the time. If you feel you are running out of time, you should guess an answer to every question. Never leave a question unanswered. Remember these tips when studying for your GED Math Exam and you’ll do great! Happy Studying!

Eliminate — get rid of the choices that are obviously incorrect

Estimate — make a quick calculation to get an approximate value or answer

Guess — give an answer without knowing for sure it is correct

Use shortcuts, such as eliminating, back–solving, and estimating Do the questions you understand first and then go back and do the hard ones. Keep an eye on the time, and if necessary, guess an answer so you fill in an answer to every question.
